The model-based PK parameters for the previously optimized saturable SC absorption model (Figure 2A (11);)) were scaled down from rat to mouse (Table 2) and the serum concentration–time profile of DFO-NPs was simulated for 8 h. To gain translational insights, model-based PK parameters were scaled up from rats to humans (Table 3) and DFO-NP disposition was simulated (Figure 3) for SC administration and compared to published PK data on native DFO given as a SC infusion in a clinical setting. (B) Model-based simulations suggested that DFO-NPs could be administered once weekly as a 25 μmol/kg large-volume SC bolus to rapidly chelate iron in the first 24 h with an additional 72–96 h of robust chelator exposure. Allometric scaling and model-based simulations were used to validate the PK model governing the absorption of disposition of DFO-NP and to subsequently predict human PK under various conditions. Allometric scaling was also used to predict the human PK of DFO-NPs in an effort to understand the viability of SC administration for first-in-human (FIH) clinical studies, and to provide some guidance for clinical formulation development. This dose is the upper limit for a reasonable formulation for SC administration, based on the key constraint of a maximum 2–3 mL SC injection volume in humans (17);) and a feasible DFO-NPs solution concentration of approximately 50 mM (or 500 mg/mL). results.content: # Calculating Human Equivalent Dosages from Animal Studies. 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗘𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗔𝗻𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀. A common mistake in translating animal study dosages to humans is using body weight scaling (mg/kg). This ignores critical differences in metabolism and physiology across species. Instead, allometric scaling—which accounts for body surface area and species-specific metabolic rates—should be used. Nair and Jacob (2016) have previously calculated conversion factors (Km ratios) for the most commonly used animals in research. The formula for Human Equivalent Dose (HED) is:. HED (mg/kg) = Animal dose (mg/kg) × Kₘ ratio. If a 200g mouse is given 10 mg of a compound:. HED (mg/kg) = (10 mg/ 0.2 kg) × 0.081 = 4.05 mg/kg for humans. Body weight alone is misleading – Smaller animals have faster metabolisms, so humans need proportionally lower doses. A simple practice guide for dose conversion between animals and humans. Title: Translational prediction of first-in-human pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of janagliflozin, a selective SGLT2 inhibitor, using allometric scaling, dedrick and PK/PD modeling methods - ScienceDirect
# Translational prediction of first-in-human pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of janagliflozin, a selective SGLT2 inhibitor, using allometric scaling, dedrick and PK/PD modeling methods. To predict human pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) characteristics of janagliflozin. Human PK parameters and profiles of janagliflozin were predicted by various methods such as allometric scaling (AS), dedrick and PK/PD modeling analysis. Predicted PK/PD characteristics of janagliflozin were applied in FIH dose design. This study predicted human PK/PD characteristics of janagliflozin based on preclinical data and provide optimal dose design for janagliflozin FIH study based on pharmacologically effective level of same class drugs. Model-based translational PK/PD prediction provided a promising approach for FIH dose design (Mager and Jusko, 2008; Yamazaki, 2013). Innovative mechanistic modeling and simulation approach have been applied in translational PK/PD predictions by taken into account of human physiological and efficacy data. In this process, we aim to predict dose of biological effect level by integrated following factors: i) Mechanistic understanding of PK/PD characteristics; ii) consideration of interspecies difference of physiology and pathophysiology; iii) exploring pharmacologically active target of same class drugs. Additionally, we will optimize FIH dose design (including starting dose and effective dose) based on predicted human PK/PD profiles and pharmacologically effective level of same class drugs. This article provided a good example of human translational PK/PD prediction and FIH dose optimization. Overall strategy of janagliflozin translational PK/PD prediction and FIH dose design was depicted in Fig. 1. Various methods were used to predict human PK/PD characteristics based on preclinical PK/PD data. In this study, we developed a model-informed translational approach for projecting first-in-human dose design by taking account of preclinical *in vivo* and *in vitro* data as well as pharmacologically active efficacy of same class drugs. This translational approach performed a good predicted PK and UGE characteristics of janagliflozin in human. In this study, we successfully processed translational PK/PD prediction of janagliflozin and optimally designed MABEL dose and PAD for first in human study. Preclinical *in vitro* and *in vivo* PK/PD data of janagliflozin, preclinical and clinical PK/PD data of three same class drugs were involved in this translational process. Based on the physiological alterations in cirrhosis or RI patients, the T2DM model was applied to predict the janagliflozin PK in these patients.

results.title: Using Allometric Scaling to Predict Human PK from Animals
results.content:
Title: Using Allometric Scaling to Predict Human PK from Animals
# Using Allometric Scaling to Predict Human PK from Animals. Allometric scaling is a powerful tool used in pharmacokinetics (PK) to predict human drug behavior based on animal data. It's founded on the principle that physiological and biological processes scale predictably with body size across different species. Basic Principles of Allometric Scaling. Allometric scaling relies on mathematical models that correlate biological parameters with body size. The power of this approach is that it considers the inherent biological similarities between species, making it a reliable method for extrapolating data from animals to humans. In pharmacokinetics, allometric scaling is used to predict parameters such as clearance, volume of distribution, and half-life of drugs. By using data from preclinical animal studies, researchers can develop an initial PK profile for a drug, which helps in designing early-phase clinical trials. Allometric scaling offers several advantages in drug development. Additionally, allometric scaling provides a scientifically grounded method to anticipate potential challenges in drug metabolism and clearance. Despite its benefits, allometric scaling is not without challenges. Variability in drug metabolism due to genetic or environmental factors can also affect scaling outcomes. Several successful applications of allometric scaling highlight its value in pharmacokinetics. For instance, in the development of oncology drugs, scaling has been used to predict human dosing from rodent models, leading to successful clinical outcomes. Similarly, in cardiovascular drug development, allometric scaling has aided in optimizing dosing regimens for better therapeutic efficacy. The future of allometric scaling in pharmacokinetics looks promising, with advancements in computational modeling and systems biology. Integrating allometric scaling with these technologies could enhance prediction accuracy and provide deeper insights into interspecies differences. As the pharmaceutical industry continues to evolve, allometric scaling remains a cornerstone method in translating animal data into human predictions. Allometric scaling serves as a vital bridge between preclinical and clinical drug development. By leveraging the natural scaling relationships between species, researchers can predict human pharmacokinetics efficiently, reducing the time and resources needed for drug development. As technology advances, the integration of allometric scaling with other predictive tools will surely refine its accuracy and applicability, ensuring its place as a key strategy in pharmacokinetics.

results.title: Advantages of Allometric Scaling Methods for Predicting Human Pharmacokinetics of Novel JAK Inhibitor -Baricitinib and Dose Extrapolation – Biomedical and Pharmacology Journal
results.content: Methods: The literature published pharmacokinetic parameters (Cl and Vd) of preclinical species (Rat, Dog and monkey) were utilized for the allometry scaling of Baricitinib. The connection among the primary pharmacokinetic parameters [Volume of distribution (Vd) and clearance (Cl)] and body weight (BW) were studied across three preclinical species, we used the double logarithmic plots for prediction of the human pharmacokinetic parameters i.e. Cl and Vd with use of simple allometry and with additional correction factors for better prediction. Results: By application of the allometric scaling methods and principles correlation was found to be satisfactory for the prediction of intravenous human Cl and Vd for baricitinib. The volume of distribution (Vd) predicted by simple allometry (65.3 L) was found to be in agreement with the reported value (75.5 L); clearance (Cl) prediction by simple allometry was found to be at least 1.06 -closer to the reported value (245 mL/min); CF were used to predict the clearance.
